description: A LINK to one material file in Library/Materials. Wire it into a 3D Render row's green endpoint to give that primitive a material.
instructions:
The material twin of the Parametric Object node: it holds no geometry and computes nothing — it names a FILE and publishes that name, so a material is edited in one place and referenced from many.

WIRING. Every 3D Render row grows a second, GREEN target endpoint (`matin-<rowId>`) beside its amber geometry one. Amber carries the row's face list, green carries its material. They are separate planes on purpose: the same material feeds a dozen rows across a dozen objects, while a face list belongs to exactly one row.

PATH is Library-relative and includes the folder — "Materials/Masonry/brick.json". The file is resolved by whoever renders: nothing is inlined into the object, so retuning brick.json restyles every row that points at it without touching a single .pobj.

WHAT A MATERIAL FILE HOLDS (schema `material/1`) — one flat recipe per renderer, never a serialised shader graph:
• `procedural` — Blender's own texture-node vocabulary (brick / checker / noise / voronoi / wave / gradient / magic / white-noise) plus that node's inputs, in metres. The Blender importer expands the recipe into whatever node tree it wants; the file never describes the tree.
• `pbr` — base colour, roughness, metallic (plus transmission / IOR for glazing). The fallback for any viewer that cannot evaluate a procedural — the 3D viewport and glTF export.
• `plan2d` — the canvas hatch the 2D Render row draws: none / diagonal / dots, with spacing, angle and weight.
• `dxf` — the ACAD pattern name the DXF export writes (AR-B816, AR-CONC, GRASS …), with scale and angle.

So one name resolves to a procedural shader in Blender, a PBR colour in the viewport, a poché hatch in plan and a real hatch pattern in the drawing — the four places a material has to appear, kept in step because they are four fields of one file rather than four unrelated settings.

WITH NOTHING WIRED a row keeps its own flat colour, exactly as before. A material is additive: it never removes the row's colour, it supersedes it where a renderer can do better.
